newsitem.title: USA: BankAmerica seen wary about buying broker.
newsitem.headline: BankAmerica seen wary about buying broker.

text.p: If BankAmerica Corp decides to take another leap into the securities business it will be hoping for a more permanent relationship than its short-lived fling with Charles Schwab & Co in the 1980's.

An item in the Inside Wall Street column in Business Week said there have been talks between BankAmerica and PaineWebber Group Inc about a combination. Investors stampeded into the stock of PaineWebber Group Inc Friday, sending the stock up four to 31-3/4.
Brown Brothers Harriman analyst Raphael Soifer said BankAmerica executives discussed the possiblity of buying a broker at a meeting with analysts on Thursday.

According to Soifer, chief financial officer Michael O'Neill said that, while BankAmerica likes the equity underwriting business and believes it would take too long to build a business internally, it also finds the asking prices of Wall Street firms too high.
O'Neill said BankAmerica would not overpay for an acquisiton, the analyst said.

The article referred to "extensive and detailed" talks between BankAmerica chief executive David Coulter and PaineWebber chief executive Donald Marron, citing an unidentified New York investment manager.
BankAmerica bought the Charles Schwab discount brokerage in 1983 for $55 million. The deal provided capital enabling the rapidly growing firm to expand.
But during the mid-80's founder Charles Schwab and his team chafed under the regulatory backdrop that banks operate in and the business style of the banking parent.

According to a source familiar with the situation, the BankAmerica ownership posed difficulties in getting more heavily involved in mutual funds. Finally, in 1987 the founder led a $280 million management buyout. Soon after, the firm went public as Charles Schwab Corp.

Speculation about banks buying brokers have been making the rounds since last summer when the Federal Reserve proposed easing a restriction on the amount of underwriting of securities that a bank holding company can do through a subsidiary set up under Section 20 of the Glass Steagall law.

In December, the Fed approved lifting the limit on the amount of underwriting to 25 of the gross the amount of gross revenue of the securities unit. The new rule, which raises the limit from 10 percent, takes effect in March.

Many banking firms have not been sitting around waiting for the rules to change. J.P. Morgan & Co Inc has stood out as a company that has built up a huge securities business internally. The efforts are generally considered to be a big success.

At a briefing on Thursday following the release of its quarterly earnings, First Union Corp's chief financial officer Robert Atwood said the firm has brought about a successful marriage of a traditional "bread and butter banking business" with Wall Street investment banking. The Charlotte, N.C.-based bank holding company has been building its investment business internally and has made acquistions in the investment management area. Both BankAmerica and PaineWebber declined comment on the Business Week story.
